english.html: If you know it not, the eyes are the guides in love (Si nescis, oculi sunt in amore duces).

notes.original: Properce an liure ij. des ele gies.
notes.gloss: The note is printed on p021 beside the verse; its marker stands at the foot of p020.

english.html: And that is why Juvenal thinks it a prodigious and too strange thing that a blind man should be in love. And Martial mocks Codrus, who, deprived of sight, nevertheless afterwards became extremely passionate for the love of a woman.
No one in all the city gives more credit than Codrus. Since he is so poor, how so? Blind, he loves (Plus credit nemo, quam tota Codrus in urbe, / Cum sit tam pauper, quomodo? caecus amat). c

notes.gloss: Martial's point is a pun: credit is "gives credit, lends," and caecus amat means Codrus loves blindly — he is not blind. Coras takes caecus literally; the Juvenal passage on the blind lover has not been located.

english.html: And to whom the said du Tilh had given several private and particular tokens, even of the acts and words which pass most secretly between married people, and which others cannot well know or understand — so far as to tell her the places, times and hours of the secret acts of marriage (much easier to understand than honest to recite or write), and the words which, before, after and during the act, they had exchanged — had likewise persuaded herself, with the others, that the said du Tilh was certainly Martin Guerre her husband.

The wife of Q. Sertorius at Rome, and Jeanne, daughter of Count Baldwin of Flanders, were a little better advised: for when the man who called himself the son of Q. Sertorius, and was followed by many as such at Rome, one day presented himself to the wife of Sertorius as to his mother, giving her very familiar, and nevertheless secret and true, tokens, she with great pertinacity and virtuous

uncertain.note: Both reads set continues_prev true, assuming the hexameter of the Propertius couplet stood at the foot of p020. p020's final line is prose ('me dit Properce, ſont les guides, chefs & cõducteurs {b}.'), so this pentameter is quoted alone after a full stop; continues_prev set false. Paragraph block per §6

No marker b in the body of this page: the note with key b is printed at the top of the margin, beside body line 2. Its marker {b} is the last marker on p020 (final line 'me dit Properce, ſont les guides, chefs & cõducteurs {b}.'). Recorded here as a note without a body marker

Printed 'an' (sic): the sort after 'a' is joined at the top (arch) and open at the foot, unlike the italic u of 'liure' on the next line. A turned u for 'au liure ij.'; transcribed as printed. B read 'au' by sense; reconciled from the glyph

Same word as in note b, heavily inked; the top join is the likeliest reading, so 'an' (sic, turned u for 'au') as in note b. 'au' remains possible under the blot. Pointer: pages/full/p021.jpg x≈2150-2450, y≈1030-1090 (margin beside the Martial couplet)

uncertain.note: 'quomodo!' — the mark is a vertical stroke over a point, i.e. an exclamation, not the question mark the received text of Martial III.15 has. Transcribed as printed (sic); could conceivably be a damaged '?'.
